rules.name: AWS Access Key
rules.why: AWS Access Keys grant direct access to your cloud services and resources.
rules.scenario: An attacker who finds the key can launch servers, read S3 buckets, and delete data on your behalf — charges and breaches may go unnoticed for days.
rules.fix: Use environment variables or AWS IAM roles instead. Rotate the key immediately via the AWS Console and audit CloudTrail for unauthorized usage.

rules.name: OpenAI API Key
rules.why: An OpenAI API key in source code can be used by anyone who reads the repository — including forks and search engine caches.
rules.scenario: Automated scanners harvest OpenAI keys from GitHub within minutes of a push. Usage costs can reach thousands of dollars before the key is revoked.
rules.fix: Store in a .env file (with .env in .gitignore) or in your platform's secret manager. Revoke the exposed key at platform.openai.com/api-keys.

rules.name: GitHub Personal Access Token
rules.why: GitHub tokens grant access to your repositories and organization settings, scoped to whatever permissions were granted at creation.
rules.scenario: With a valid token, an attacker can read private code, push commits, create webhooks, or inject malicious code into your repository.
rules.fix: Use GitHub Actions secrets for CI/CD: ${{ secrets.MY_TOKEN }}. Revoke the exposed token immediately at github.com/settings/tokens.

rules.name: Generic API Key (hardcoded)
rules.why: Hardcoded API keys are exposed to everyone who can read the source code — including all contributors, contractors, and anyone who gains repository access.
rules.scenario: If the repository is shared with a consultant or accidentally made public, the API key is immediately exposed to external parties.
rules.fix: Move to an environment variable: process.env.API_KEY or the equivalent for your language. Store the value in a .env file excluded from git, or use a secrets manager.

rules.name: Hardcoded password
rules.why: Hardcoded passwords in source code are one of the most common vulnerabilities in AI-generated code. They end up in version control history permanently — even after deletion.
rules.scenario: An AI coding tool fills in a sample password that gets committed and forgotten. Anyone with repository access — including future contributors — can see it forever in git history.
rules.fix: Use environment variables or a secrets manager. Ensure .env is in .gitignore. For .NET: use Web.config encrypted sections or environment variables via ConfigurationManager.

rules.name: Private key (PEM format)
rules.why: A private key in source code compromises your entire cryptographic infrastructure — SSL certificates, SSH access, and signed tokens can all be forged.
rules.scenario: The committed private key is used to decrypt TLS traffic captured by an attacker, or to sign malicious code as if it came from your organisation.
rules.fix: Private keys must never appear in source code. Store in a secrets manager or HSM. Revoke and reissue the affected certificate or key pair immediately.

rules.name: Hardcoded JWT secret
rules.why: The JWT signing secret is used to sign and verify all authentication tokens. Exposing it allows an attacker to forge valid sessions for any user.
rules.scenario: An attacker who knows the secret creates a JWT with admin: true and any user ID, bypassing all authentication checks in your application.
rules.fix: Generate a strong random secret (minimum 256 bits) and store it in an environment variable. Rotate the secret and invalidate all existing sessions immediately.

rules.name: Stripe Secret Key
rules.why: Stripe live keys grant full programmatic access to your payment account, including initiating payouts, refunds, and reading card data.
rules.scenario: An attacker uses the exposed key to initiate payouts to an external account or enumerate customer payment methods.
rules.fix: Never use live keys in source code. Store in a server-side environment variable only. Revoke the exposed key immediately in the Stripe Dashboard and audit recent API activity.
